prompt: Add a follow camera with drag margins so small player movements do not move the view.

config.plan_model: Agent-tool model parameter 'sonnet' (Claude Code sub-agent; the harness did not report the resolved model id)
config.how: one fresh general-purpose sub-agent per plan, reads a job file with project brief + the developer prompt, writes numbered plan (<=8 steps, no code) via Write; not Claude Code plan mode

plans.text:
1. Open level_01.tscn and check how the Player is placed in the scene tree and whether any camera already exists. Note the level's size and the tile layer's extents so the camera limits can match them.
2. Add a Camera2D as a child of the Player node so it follows automatically, and make sure it is the current camera. Keep the camera's rotation and zoom at their defaults for now.
3. Enable drag margin smoothing on the camera and turn on the horizontal and vertical drag margins. Set the horizontal margin wider than the vertical one, since a platformer mostly moves sideways, and keep both small enough that the player cannot reach the screen edge.
4. Set the camera limits (left, right, top, bottom) from the TileMapLayer's used rectangle so the view never shows empty space outside the level. Decide whether to set these in the editor or from a small level script that reads the tile bounds.
5. Optionally enable position smoothing with a modest speed so the camera glides when it does move, and tune it so it does not lag behind fast jumps or falls. Check that the drag margin and smoothing settings do not fight each other.
6. Check player.gd and the enemy scenes for anything that assumes a fixed view, such as screen-coordinate math or off-screen despawn checks. Update those to use world coordinates if needed.
7. Run level_01.tscn and test standing still, small side-to-side steps, long runs, jumps, and falls. Confirm small movements leave the view still and larger ones move it smoothly.
8. Tune the margin sizes, smoothing speed, and limits based on the playtest, and save the finished scene.

1. Open level_01.tscn and check whether a camera already exists in the level or under the Player, so I extend it rather than add a duplicate.
2. Add a Camera2D as a child of the Player node (so it follows automatically) and make sure it is the current camera for the level.
3. Enable the drag margin settings on the Camera2D for both horizontal and vertical axes, and start with modest margins so small movements stay inside the dead zone.
4. Tune the horizontal and vertical margins separately: wider horizontally for left/right running, narrower vertically so jumps and falls still track reasonably.
5. Set camera limits (left, right, top, bottom) to match the extents of the TileMapLayer so the view never shows empty space beyond the level.
6. Decide on smoothing: leave position smoothing off at first, then optionally enable it with a gentle speed if movement feels abrupt when the player leaves the dead zone.
7. Run level_01 and playtest walking in place, small jumps, long runs, and falls, adjusting margins until tiny movements do not shift the view but real travel does.
8. Confirm the camera behaves in both enemy-heavy areas and at level edges, and that no other scene (enemies, tilemap) has a conflicting camera or script affecting the view.

1. Open level_01.tscn and review how the Player is placed and whether any camera already exists in the level or inside the Player scene. Note the level's extent from the TileMapLayer so the camera can be bounded later.
2. Add a Camera2D as a child of the Player node so it follows automatically, rather than writing a separate tracking script. Make sure it is the active camera for the scene.
3. Enable the Camera2D's drag margin settings for horizontal and vertical movement. Choose small margin values so the player can move inside a dead zone without shifting the view.
4. Tune the horizontal and vertical margins separately, with a tighter vertical zone or a slightly larger one depending on how much jumping should shift the view. Keep them symmetric left/right and top/bottom unless the game feel calls for otherwise.
5. Turn on position smoothing with a modest speed so that when the margin is exceeded the camera eases to the player instead of snapping.
6. Set camera limits (left, right, top, bottom) from the TileMapLayer's used area so the view never shows empty space beyond the level edges.
7. Check that the camera does not interfere with player.gd, the CollisionShape2D, or the enemy scenes, and that the camera is not duplicated if the Player is instantiated elsewhere.
8. Run level_01 and playtest: stand still, make small steps, jump, and run to the edges, then adjust margins, smoothing and limits until small movements leave the view still and large ones scroll naturally.

1. Review level_01.tscn and the Player scene to confirm the node layout, the level's extents, and how player.gd moves the CharacterBody2D (including any jump or fall behavior that affects vertical camera feel).
2. Decide where the camera lives: add a Camera2D as a child of the Player so it follows automatically, keeping it in the Player scene so every level that instances the player gets it.
3. Enable the camera as current and set its position smoothing so movement feels fluid rather than snapping.
4. Turn on drag margin handling for both horizontal and vertical axes, and choose small initial margin values so the player can move within a dead zone before the view shifts. Use a wider horizontal margin than vertical so jumps do not constantly bob the view.
5. Set the camera limits (left, right, top, bottom) to match the level's bounds based on the TileMapLayer's used area, so the view never shows empty space outside the level.
6. Make sure the camera does not inherit unwanted behavior, such as rotation or the sprite's flip, and that the drag margin settings do not conflict with any scripted camera offsets in player.gd.
7. Run level_01 and test by making small steps, full runs, jumps, and falls to verify that tiny movements leave the view still and larger movements scroll it smoothly, including near the level edges.
8. Tune the margin and smoothing values based on that playtest, and optionally expose them as exported properties or note the final values so other levels can reuse them.

1. Open level_01.tscn and check how the Player is placed in the scene tree and whether any camera or view-related node already exists, so the new camera does not conflict with it.
2. Add a Camera2D as a child of the Player node so it follows automatically, and make sure it is the current camera for the level.
3. Enable the drag margin settings on the Camera2D and turn on both horizontal and vertical drag. Start with modest margins on each side so small movements stay inside the dead zone and do not scroll the view.
4. Set the drag margins asymmetrically if useful (for example a smaller vertical margin than horizontal) so jumping does not cause constant vertical scrolling while walking still feels responsive.
5. Configure the camera limits (left, right, top, bottom) to match the TileMapLayer bounds so the view never shows empty space beyond the level edges.
6. Consider enabling position smoothing with a gentle speed so the camera glides when it does move, and verify it does not fight with the drag margins.
7. Run level_01.tscn and test walking, jumping, falling, and standing near level edges. Confirm small movements leave the view still and larger movements pull the camera along.
8. Tune the margin sizes and smoothing values from play-testing, and confirm the camera behaves correctly after respawn or scene reload.

1. Review level_01.tscn and the Player scene to confirm the Player's node path, sprite size, and the level's overall bounds so the camera has a clear target and limits.
2. Add a Camera2D node as a child of the Player in the Player scene, so it follows automatically without any script-driven position syncing.
3. Make that camera the active one and set its anchor to the player's center, checking that no other camera exists in the level or enemy scenes that could conflict.
4. Enable the horizontal and vertical drag margin settings on the Camera2D, then choose small left/right/top/bottom margin values so minor movement stays inside the dead zone.
5. Set the vertical margins larger than the horizontal ones if needed, so ordinary jumping does not make the view bob up and down.
6. Set the camera limits to the edges of the TileMapLayer's used area so the view never shows empty space beyond the level.
7. Optionally enable position smoothing with a modest speed so the view eases once the player leaves the dead zone instead of snapping.
8. Run level_01 and playtest walking, jumping, and falling near the level edges, then tune margins, smoothing, and limits until the feel is right and enemies and tiles still render correctly.

1. Review level_01.tscn and player.gd to confirm how the Player is instanced, its coordinate space, and whether any existing camera or scene-level scripts already manage the view.
2. Add a Camera2D as a child of the Player node so it follows automatically, and make sure it is the current camera for the level.
3. Enable the drag margin settings on the Camera2D and set horizontal and vertical margins so the player can move within a small central dead zone before the view scrolls. Start with modest values and tune later.
4. Decide on the vertical behavior: use a smaller or zero vertical drag margin if jumps should not bounce the view, and keep a wider horizontal margin for walking.
5. Set camera limits (left, right, top, bottom) from the TileMapLayer's used area so the view never shows empty space beyond the level edges.
6. Consider enabling position smoothing with a gentle speed so the camera glides when it does move, and confirm it does not conflict with the drag margins or cause jitter with the player's physics movement.
7. Run level_01.tscn and playtest: walk in place, make small jumps, run to the edges, and check that small movements leave the view still while larger ones scroll it.
8. Tune the margin, smoothing, and limit values based on playtesting, then verify the camera behaves correctly if the Player is respawned or the level is reloaded.

1. Review level_01.tscn and player.gd to confirm how the Player is positioned, how fast it moves, and the level's pixel bounds. Note the viewport size and tile size so camera values can be tuned to them.
2. Add a Camera2D to the scene as a child of the Player (or as a sibling that tracks it), so it follows the Player automatically. Make it the current camera and give it a clear name such as FollowCamera.
3. Enable the drag margin settings on the Camera2D for horizontal and vertical movement. Choose small margins for the horizontal axis and a somewhat different margin for the vertical axis, so tiny movements and small hops stay inside the dead zone.
4. Set the left, right, top, and bottom drag margin values independently, since platformers usually want a wider horizontal dead zone and a tighter vertical one. Keep the margins symmetrical at first, then adjust after playtesting.
5. Set camera limits (left, top, right, bottom) to match the level's bounds based on the TileMapLayer extents, so the view never shows empty space past the level edges.
6. Add optional position smoothing with a modest speed so the camera eases to the player once the margin is exceeded instead of snapping.
7. Verify the camera is not duplicated in the enemy scenes and that no other Camera2D is set as current. Confirm the setup works if the Player is respawned or the level is reloaded.
8. Playtest level_01.tscn by making small movements, jumping, and running across the level, and tune the margin and smoothing values until small movements leave the view still and larger ones scroll it smoothly.

1. Review level_01.tscn and the Player node setup to confirm where the camera should live and how large the level is. Decide whether the camera will be a child of Player or a separate node that follows it.
2. Add a Camera2D node as a child of the Player in level_01.tscn so it tracks the player's position automatically. Make sure it is set as the current camera for the level.
3. Enable drag margin behavior on the Camera2D by turning on horizontal and vertical drag. Set the left, right, top, and bottom margins to small fractions so minor movement stays inside the dead zone.
4. Tune the margins asymmetrically if needed, for example a wider horizontal dead zone and a smaller vertical one, so jumping on platforms feels natural.
5. Set camera limits (left, right, top, bottom) to match the level bounds from the TileMapLayer so the view never shows empty space beyond the level.
6. Optionally enable position smoothing with a modest speed so camera motion is not jarring when the player leaves the dead zone. Keep it subtle to avoid input lag.
7. Check that the camera does not interfere with the player's script or the enemy scenes, and that the camera is not duplicated in other scenes.
8. Playtest level_01 by walking, jumping, and falling, and adjust margins, smoothing, and limits until small movements leave the view still and larger ones scroll it smoothly.

1. Review level_01.tscn and the Player node's position in the scene tree to decide where the camera belongs, and check that player.gd does not already move or reparent any camera.
2. Add a Camera2D as a child of the Player node in level_01.tscn so it follows the player automatically, and set it as the current camera.
3. Enable the camera's drag margin behavior for both horizontal and vertical axes, and set the horizontal and vertical drag margins to small fractions of the screen so minor player movement stays inside the dead zone.
4. Choose separate values for the left, right, top, and bottom margins; for example, a wider horizontal dead zone and a tighter vertical one so jumps do not cause constant vertical scrolling.
5. Set the camera limits (left, right, top, bottom) to match the bounds of the TileMapLayer in the level so the view never shows empty space beyond the level edges.
6. Consider enabling position smoothing with a modest speed so the camera glides when it does start to move, and make sure it does not fight the drag margins.
7. Run level_01 and test walking in small steps, jumping, falling off platforms, and moving fast, adjusting the margins until small movements leave the view still and large movements scroll it comfortably.
8. Check that both enemy scenes and any on-screen UI still behave correctly with the moving camera, and that the player sprite and collisions do not jitter or show pixel shimmer.
